analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying Congress for life.
analysis.headline: A bill making it a crime for former senators and representatives to ever lobby Congress was introduced in February 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The BLAST Act would change the existing 'cooling-off' rule, which bars former senators from lobbying for two years and former House members for one year, into a lifetime ban. Any former senator, representative, or elected congressional officer who contacts Congress to influence legislation on someone else's behalf would face criminal penalties under the same law that punishes federal bribery-related offenses. The bill never moved beyond its initial committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who currently share a Congress with former colleagues who can walk the halls and sell their access to the highest-paying clients after only one or two years out of office. A permanent ban would shrink the market for selling a former member's relationships and inside knowledge.

how_it_helps.text: The bill converts the current post-employment lobbying ban — two years for former senators, one year for former House members and elected officers — into a permanent prohibition [S2].
It writes the ban into the criminal code and subjects violators to the penalties in section 216 of title 18, the statute used to punish federal bribery-related conflicts of interest [S3].

The restriction applies to any communication or appearance before a current member, officer, or employee of either house of Congress, made with intent to influence on behalf of anyone other than the United States [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would lose the ability to monetize their congressional relationships for life, and the lobbying firms and interest groups that hire them precisely for those relationships.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban is far broader than most state revolving-door rules and broader than the existing federal ban, and a good-faith objection is that it could deter people from running for Congress at all by making the office a one-way door [S2].

The bill criminalizes a form of petitioning the government, and it applies only to former members and elected officers — not to the thousands of congressional staff who also leave and lobby, leaving a large revolving door open [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A permanent ban would meaningfully close the best-known route by which former lawmakers sell influence, at the cost of a rule that is stricter than what most reformers propose and that leaves staff lobbying untouched. The one-sided scope and the possibility of discouraging candidates are real design weaknesses, but the core idea — that a former senator's phone call should not be for sale forever — is hard to argue against on the merits. The bill's failure was not a judgment on those tradeoffs: it never received any hearing or debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Constitution subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Trey Hollingsworth (R-IN) introduced the BLAST Act on February 26, 2021 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 28, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it remained with no further action recorded [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor over the bill's lifetime [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying firms that hire them, who keep the existing one- and two-year cooling-off windows and the ability to sell congressional access afterward; the House Judiciary Committee leadership also never had to take a position.

for.name: Rep. Trey Hollingsworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it was his only recorded action on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat at subcommittee referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor was a Republican and no member of either party cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.note: Firms hire former senators and representatives for their relationships and knowledge of how Congress works; a permanent ban removes their most valuable hires. That loss is the public's gain, since it reduces the market for selling a former lawmaker's influence.
The bill would bar former senators, representatives, and elected officers from ever lobbying Congress on someone else's behalf, ending a career path that currently opens after one or two years.
